A.text: Yellow watermelons simply lack lycopene, the pigment that turns ordinary melons red inside.
Watermelon flesh is about ninety-two percent water, which is why it hydrates so fast.
A cut watermelon never gets sweeter off the vine — the plant stops moving sugar into it at harvest.
Citrulline, an amino acid studied for muscle recovery, concentrates in the rind just under the green skin.
Seedless watermelons are triploid — three sets of chromosomes make their seeds sterile.
Hollow, honeycomb centers form when pollination fails partway through the fruit's growth.
Puffy, misshapen melons usually mean too few bee visits during the short bloom window.
Watermelons started in the Kalahari region of southern Africa, where wild bitter relatives still grow.
Archaeologists find watermelon seeds in ancient Egyptian sites, evidence of early cultivation.
The rind stripes are only skin-deep — flesh color has nothing to do with the pattern outside.

B.text: A deep, hollow thump when tapped usually means the melon ripened evenly all the way through.
The creamy field spot shows exactly how long the melon rested on the ground ripening.
Chilling dulls aroma — cold melon tastes flatter than the same melon served slightly cool.
Standing each half flat on its cut face stops it from rolling while you work the wedges.
Scoring the rind in shallow passes before the full cut stops thick skins from splitting sideways.
The seed cavities sit along the center line, so splitting down the middle exposes them evenly.
Vendors leave a strip of rind on each wedge as a natural handle so hands stay dry.
Ten minutes on the counter brings a chilled melon back to the temperature where its aroma returns.
A thinner blade drags less juice through the flesh than a thick chef's knife.
Freezing leftover cubes bursts the cell walls, so they turn mealy the moment they thaw.

C.text: Modern seedless varieties were largely perfected in Japan's twentieth-century breeding programs.
Japanese farmers once grew melons inside box molds, producing square fruit sold purely as gifts.
Watermelon has anchored American Southern summer gatherings for well over a century.
Egypt ranks among the world's biggest exporters, shipping melons through winter into Europe.
Spanish and Portuguese traders carried melon varieties out of Africa into Europe after the 1400s.
In parts of China, flawless melons are sold as gift fruit, priced almost entirely by appearance.
Seed-spitting contests have been a fixture of American county fairs since the early 1900s.
Watermelon rind pickles were a standard entry in American pantry cookbooks by the 1800s.
In Turkey, watermelon is commonly served as dessert alongside white cheese.
Picnic folklore claims the sweetest melons grow at patch edges, where the vines had to struggle.

D.text: Heavier melons for their size hold more juice — always compare two by weight, not size.
A yellow, creamy field spot means it ripened on the vine; white or green means it was picked early.
Dull, dark skin usually beats a glossy bright one — shine often means picked under-ripe.
Fine brown webbing on the skin marks repeated bee visits to the blossom, often a sweeter-spot sign.
Watermelon keeps best whole and cool — cut pieces start degrading within days.
Dark, hard seeds mean full maturity; pale soft seeds are simply the young, undeveloped stage.
You can cube a whole melon in under a minute by scoring a grid through the half while the rind holds it.
Salt does not add sweetness — it suppresses bitterness, so the fruit's own sugar reads stronger.
Melon balls scoop cleanly only from firm, chilled flesh; warm flesh collapses under the spoon.
The sweetest bite usually sits just above the rind, where the sugar concentrates last.
